title: School Food Exhibition Faces Scrutiny Over Unhealthy Products
text:
An investigation found that more than a third of suppliers at the UK's largest school food exhibition sold products high in fat, sugar or salt, prompting public health concerns as the government prepares tougher nutritional standards for school meals.
An investigation into the United Kingdom's largest school food trade exhibition has raised concerns about the influence of unhealthy products on the people and companies responsible for feeding children.
Researchers found that 52 of the 137 suppliers attending The School Food People Show and Forum in Birmingham offered products considered high in fat, sugar or salt. The event, which describes itself as the only national exhibition devoted entirely to school food, brings together more than 1,000 delegates from the catering sector. It is designed to help suppliers display products, establish relationships with school caterers and compete for contracts with schools and other educational institutions.
The products identified at the exhibition included hot dogs, pizzas, muffins, cakes, cookies, waffles, ice cream, chocolate bars, crisps, sweets and carbonated drinks. According to the investigation, seven wholesalers sold confectionery and snack foods, while five companies specialised in ice cream and four supplied soft drinks. Other exhibitors offered pizza products, cake mixes, vending machines stocked with sweets and specialist hot dog items.
Some drinks promoted as suitable for schools reportedly contained more than half of an adult's recommended daily sugar allowance in a single can. The investigation also found that the principal trade organisation representing school food caterers, which organises the event, receives sponsorship from businesses supplying products such as pizza, cakes, waffles and ice cream. Public health specialists and child nutrition advocates described the findings as troubling, particularly because the exhibition is closely connected to decisions about school menus.
Greg Fell, president of the Association of Directors of Public Health and director of public health for Sheffield City Council, said the event reflected an environment that could contribute to rising levels of unhealthy weight among children. Marie Murphy, an assistant professor of child and adolescent nutrition at the University of Birmingham, said the presence of so many products conflicting with nutritional guidance was shocking.
Youth food campaign group Bite Back also highlighted what it called a contradiction between the government's plans to improve school meals and the continued promotion of foods that those reforms are intended to reduce. Catering companies argue that the issue is complicated by the financial pressures involved in providing school meals. Products such as confectionery, muffins and fizzy drinks can generate relatively high profit margins, allowing caterers to offset losses from nutritious cooked meals.
Healthier dishes may cost more to prepare and can be less popular with pupils, creating a commercial incentive to continue selling snacks and sweetened drinks. Some catering providers are also concerned that children may reject healthier menus and instead bring packed lunches containing highly processed snacks from home. The concerns come as the government prepares the most significant revision of school food rules since the School Food Plan was introduced in 2013.
Under the proposed standards, deep-fried foods would be removed from school menus entirely. Pizza and sausage rolls would be restricted to no more than twice a week, while ice cream and cookies would be limited to once weekly. Desserts would have to contain at least 50 percent fruit, which would substantially reduce the availability of traditional options such as chocolate sponge and jam roly-poly.
The new requirements are expected to begin in primary schools in September 2027 and in secondary schools in September 2028, although the government has not yet explained fully how compliance will be monitored. Existing rules already limit deep-fried foods to two portions a week and require schools to provide vegetables or salad every day, alongside at least one portion of fruit. The planned changes reflect growing concern about childhood obesity, poor diet and dental health.
More than one in five children in England are overweight or living with obesity when they begin primary school, and the proportion rises to more than one in three by the time they leave. Tooth decay remains the leading reason for hospital admissions among children aged five to nine. Experts warn that continued exposure to high-fat, high-sugar and high-salt products may contribute to long-term health problems, increasing pressure on public services and creating social costs that could persist for decades
